request.user:
Brand: Midnight Ritual (@midnightritual)
Positioning: Late-night minimalism for slow living
Voice: Quiet authority. Second person, never preachy, comfortable with silence and white space.
Writing style: Short declarative sentences. Concrete nouns. One idea per slide. No hype adjectives, no exclamation marks, no emoji.
Reading level: Grade 7 (plain and unhurried)
Colour theme: background #111111, foreground #F4F4F2, accent #F4F4F2
Content pillars: Ritual design, Category creation, Brand governance, Slow marketing
Category: Branding
Topic: Why brand names with more than three syllables lose 23 percent recall after midnight
Angle: Late-night decision fatigue causes the brain to truncate unfamiliar words at three syllables, so brands like 'Lumière&Co' or 'Serendipity&Co' fade from memory when tested after 10pm versus brands with shorter names

Verified facts you may use — use no other facts:
No facts survived verification. Stay general and add no numbers.

Produce:

1. title: working title, under 80 characters. Specific, not generic.
2. hook: cover line, 6–10 words, no question marks. A claim the reader wants to argue with.
3. slides: 5 to 7 frames.
   - Slide 1: kind "cover". The hook in the headline.
   - Middle slides: alternate "statement", "list", "statistic", "quote". At least one "statistic" with a real number from the facts.
   - Final slide: kind "cta". An invitation, not a sales pitch.
   - Each slide: kicker (1–3 words), headline (under 50 characters), body (one sentence), footnote (string or null).
   - Every headline must make sense on its own — people screenshot individual slides.

4. caption: 60–140 words.
   - Line 1: the hook as a specific claim.
   - Lines 2–3: the strongest verified number or fact. Be concrete.
   - Line 4: why this is not obvious.
   - Close: plain save/send invitation. No emoji, no hashtags, no links.

5. hashtags: 6 to 9 lowercase tags prefixed with #, including #midnightritual #slowbrand. No #viral/#fyp/#explore.
6. altText: 2–4 sentences describing every frame in order, no 'image of' preamble.
7. references: one entry per fact you actually used, with the real source and an honest credibility rating.

8. qualityScore: score the post 0–100 against this rubric:
   - hook (weight 0.25) — does slide 1 stop the scroll without clickbait
- clarity (weight 0.25) — is the caption readable at the brand's reading level
- visual (weight 0.2) — do the slides alternate statement and proof so the eye resets
- hashtags (weight 0.15) — mix of niche and category tags, no banned or spammy tags
- alt (weight 0.15) — does the alt text describe every frame for a screen reader
   Scores of 95+ should be rare. List anything that must change before approval in blockers.

{
  "title": string,
  "hook": string,
  "slides": [

    "score": number,
    "summary": string,
    "criteria": [ { "id": string, "label": string, "weight": number, "score": number, "note": string } ],
    "blockers": string[]
  }
}

Review each claim below.
- supported: the claim is corroborated by a source you are confident exists and says this.
- uncertain: plausible but you cannot corroborate it.
- unsupported: no reliable basis, or the claim is too strong for the evidence.

1. The average person's working memory capacity drops significantly after 10pm, reducing the ability to process multi-syllabic brand names longer than three syllables.
   Evidence: Cognitive load increases by approximately 18-22% in late-night hours, according to a 2022 study on circadian rhythm effects on working memory.
   Source: Circadian Modulation of Working Memory Capacity During Late-Night Hours — Scientific Reports (Nature Publishing Group) (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-23456-9) [medium confidence]
2. Decision fatigue impairs phonological processing, making consumers truncate complex brand names by the third syllable when exposed after midnight.
   Evidence: A 2021 neuroimaging study found that late-night exposure to polysyllabic stimuli reduced retention accuracy by 23.4% compared to morning exposure.
   Source: Decision Fatigue and Phonological Truncation: A Late-Night Consumer Behavior Study — Journal of Consumer Psychology (https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-consumer-psychology) [medium confidence]
3. Brands with names exceeding three syllables experience measurably lower unaided recall rates when participants view advertisements after 10pm versus before 6pm.
   Evidence: 2023 meta-analysis of 14 sleep-cycle advertising experiments showed a 17.8% average decline in recall for longer brand names during late-night exposure windows.
   Source: Sleep Cycle Timing and Brand Recall: A Meta-Analytic Review of 14 Late-Night Advertising Experiments — Journal of Applied Psychology (SAGE) (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022243723115500) [medium confidence]
4. The brain's phonological loop, responsible for holding verbal information, operates with reduced efficiency between 10pm and 2am, particularly affecting retention of unfamiliar multi-syllable words.
   Evidence: 2020 EEG study recorded a 29% reduction in phonological loop activation amplitude during late-night hours when participants were exposed to unfamiliar brand names.
   Source: EEG Correlates of Phonological Loop Efficiency Across the Sleep-Wake Cycle — NeuroImage (Elsevier) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053811920304567) [medium confidence]
5. Marketing research firm Mintel reported in 2022 that brands with shorter, simpler names (one to three syllables) maintain higher recall rates in late-night digital advertising campaigns.
   Evidence: Analysis of 200+ late-night digital ad campaigns found 2.3x higher click-through rates for brands with names under three syllables during post-10pm windows.
   Source: Late-Night Digital Advertising: Optimizing Brand Names for Post-10pm Engagement — Mintel Reports (https://reports.mintel.com/display/947798/) [low confidence]

- Source URLs listed may not contain the exact studies described; titles and publishers should be cross-checked for accuracy.
- The application of these cognitive findings specifically to brand recall in late-night contexts requires direct experimental validation.
- The 2023 meta-analysis citation appears generic; the actual number of studies and specific results need verification.

Topic: Mexico City's 2024-2025 ciclovía expansion added 87 km of protected bike lanes but shifted crash severity from minor injuries to fatal intersections
Angle: When Mexico City widened protected bike lanes from 42 km to 129 km between 2024 and 2025, intersection fatalities rose 34 percent even as overall cyclist injuries dropped 18 percent — the safety gain came from rerouting crashes onto arterials with no signal timing adjustments

Verified facts you may use — use no other facts:
1. Mexico City's 2024-2025 ciclovía expansion increased protected bike lane infrastructure from 42 km to 129 km, adding exactly 87 km of new lanes.
   Evidence: The Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes reported that the red de ciclovías protegidas grew from 42 km to 129 km between December 2024 and December 2025, an increase of 87 km through new and upgraded corridors.
   Source: Red de Ciclovías Protegidas: Avance 2025 — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.movi.gob.mx/docs/ciclovias-protegidas-2025.pdf) [high confidence]
2. Despite the lane expansion, cyclist injury severity increased at intersections, with reported intersection-related cyclist fatalities rising 34 percent during the 2024-2025 period.
   Evidence: According to official crash statistics published in the Movilidad Segura annual report, cyclist fatalities occurring at signalized and unsignalized intersections rose from 61 in 2024 to 82 in 2025, a 34.4 percent increase.
   Source: Informe Movilidad Segura 2025: Estadísticas de Accidentes Viales — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.movi.gob.mx/docs/movilidad-segura-2025-estadisticas.pdf) [medium confidence]
3. Overall cyclist injuries dropped 18 percent after the 2024-2025 expansion, suggesting the new lanes reduced non-intersection crashes but displaced risk to intersections.
   Evidence: Total reported cyclist injuries decreased from 2,847 in 2024 to 2,335 in 2025, an 18.0 percent reduction, according to the same Movilidad Segura dataset.
   Source: Informe Movilidad Segura 2025: Estadísticas de Accidentes Viales — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.movi.gob.mx/docs/movilidad-segura-2025-estadisticas.pdf) [medium confidence]
4. Of all cyclist fatalities recorded in 2025, 73 percent occurred at intersections lacking adaptive signal timing adjustments for the new protected lane network.
   Evidence: The 2025 crash analysis indicated that 60 of the 82 cyclist fatalities (73.2 percent) took place at intersections where traffic light phasing had not been modified to accommodate the parallel protected bike lane corridors added that year.
   Source: Análisis de Siniestralidad Vial de Ciclistas 2025 — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.movi.gob.mx/docs/analisis-siniestralidad-ciclistas-2025.pdf) [medium confidence]
5. City officials acknowledged in a November 2025 press briefing that no intersection signal retiming was programmed for the 2024-2025 ciclovía expansion projects.
   Evidence: At a 20 November 2025 press conference, Movilidad official Gabriela López stated that signal synchronization upgrades were not included in the expansion budget and remained pending for a 2026 works cycle.
   Source: Conferencia de Prensa: Actualización de Corredores Ciclistas 2025 — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=clave2025ciclovias) [high confidence]
6. The 87 km expansion concentrated 64 percent of new protected lanes on arterial roads that diverted cyclists from calmer residential routes into higher-speed traffic corridors.
   Evidence: Of the 87 additional kilometers added, 56 km (64.4 percent) were installed on classified arterial routes such as Eje 4 Sur and Avenida de los Insurgentes Sur, according to the 2025 infrastructure inventory.
   Source: Inventario de Infraestructura Ciclista 2025 — Secretaría de Movilidad y Transportes de la Ciudad de México (https://www.movi.gob.mx/docs/inventario-ciclista-2025.pdf) [high confidence]

Produce:

1. title: working title, under 80 characters. Specific, not generic.
2. hook: cover line, 6–10 words, no question marks. A claim the reader wants to argue with.
3. slides: 5 to 7 frames.
   - Slide 1: kind "cover". The hook in the headline.
   - Middle slides: alternate "statement", "list", "statistic", "quote". At least one "statistic" with a real number from the facts.
   - Final slide: kind "cta". An invitation, not a sales pitch.
   - Each slide: kicker (1–3 words), headline (under 50 characters), body (one sentence), footnote (string or null).
   - Every headline must make sense on its own — people screenshot individual slides.

4. caption: 60–140 words.
   - Line 1: the hook as a specific claim.
   - Lines 2–3: the strongest verified number or fact. Be concrete.
   - Line 4: why this is not obvious.
   - Close: plain save/send invitation. No emoji, no hashtags, no links.

5. hashtags: 6 to 9 lowercase tags prefixed with #, including #studionoir #citydesign. No #viral/#fyp/#explore.
6. altText: 2–4 sentences describing every frame in order, no 'image of' preamble.
7. references: one entry per fact you actually used, with the real source and an honest credibility rating.

slides.headline: This is for the geography team that is tired of reinventing.
slides.body: The urban systems myth that holds teams back — and what actually works.

slides.headline: "Good urban systems is intuition"
slides.body: Most geography brands believe great decisions come from instinct. They are wrong.

slides.headline: Intuition fails 73% of the time under pressure
slides.body: Teams that document their reasoning make 2.4× faster decisions in the next quarter.

slides.headline: Name the trade-off
slides.body: Every urban systems decision is a trade-off. Write down what you chose and what you gave up.

slides.headline: Set the constraint
slides.body: A urban systems rule without a boundary is just an opinion. Add a number, a deadline, or a threshold.

slides.headline: Save this and try it this week
slides.body: Pick one urban systems decision you have been putting off. Write the rule, share it, and see what changes.

parsed.caption:
The urban systems struggle is real — and solvable.

Here is what Studio Noir has learned: every decision that survives a busy quarter was documented before the quarter started. Not in a slide deck. In a sentence someone can quote.
parsed.altText: 6-frame carousel in Studio Noir's palette (#FFFFFF background, #111111 type). Frame 1: Cover slide — Infrastructure economics — the data behind great decisions. Frame 2: Statement — "Good urban systems is intuition". Frame 3: Statistic — Intuition fails 73% of the time under pressure. Frame 4: Rule — Name the trade-off. Frame 5: Rule — Set the constraint. Frame 6: Call to action — Save this and try it this week.

Angle: After studying 50 geography teams, this pattern emerged.

1. Urban systems decisions are only useful when someone has written down the rule behind them.
   Evidence: Offline engine: no sources were consulted, so this is a prompt for research rather than a finding.

   Evidence: Offline engine: no sources were consulted, so this is a prompt for research rather than a finding.
   Source: Not researched — Offline engine (no url) [low confidence]

   Evidence: Offline engine: no sources were consulted, so this is a prompt for research rather than a finding.
   Source: Not researched — Offline engine (no url) [low confidence]

Produce:

1. title: working title, under 80 characters. Specific, not generic.
2. hook: cover line, 6–10 words, no question marks. A claim the reader wants to argue with.
3. slides: 5 to 7 frames.
   - Slide 1: kind "cover". The hook in the headline.
   - Middle slides: alternate "statement", "list", "statistic", "quote". At least one "statistic" with a real number from the facts.
   - Final slide: kind "cta". An invitation, not a sales pitch.
   - Each slide: kicker (1–3 words), headline (under 50 characters), body (one sentence), footnote (string or null).
   - Every headline must make sense on its own — people screenshot individual slides.

4. caption: 60–140 words.
   - Line 1: the hook as a specific claim.
   - Lines 2–3: the strongest verified number or fact. Be concrete.
   - Line 4: why this is not obvious.
   - Close: plain save/send invitation. No emoji, no hashtags, no links.

5. hashtags: 6 to 9 lowercase tags prefixed with #, including #studionoir #citydesign. No #viral/#fyp/#explore.
6. altText: 2–4 sentences describing every frame in order, no 'image of' preamble.
7. references: one entry per fact you actually used, with the real source and an honest credibility rating.

   - hook (weight 0.25) — does slide 1 stop the scroll without clickbait
- clarity (weight 0.25) — is the caption readable at the brand's reading level
- visual (weight 0.2) — do the slides alternate statement and proof so the eye resets
- hashtags (weight 0.15) — mix of niche and category tags, no banned or spammy tags
- alt (weight 0.15) — does the alt text describe every frame for a screen reader
   Scores of 95+ should be rare. List anything that must change before approval in blockers.

Collect 4 to 8 facts that support the angle. For each fact:
- state the claim as a specific, arguable sentence (not a vague generalization),
- add the evidence behind it (a number, a study result, a named decision),
- name the specific source (title, publisher, canonical url),
- set confidence honestly: high only when you are confident the source exists and says this.

Quality criteria for facts:

- Prefer named sources (Harvard, McKinsey, a specific company) over anonymous ones.
- Each fact should be useful on its own — someone could pull it out and share it.

Then list genuine gaps: what a careful editor should double-check before publishing.
